item.title: Only 16% of Telecom AI Initiatives Reach Production, Study Finds
item.dc:creator: Leland McFarland
item.description: Discover the insights from a recent study revealing that only 16% of telecom AI initiatives successfully reach production. Explore the challenges and opportunities in the telecom sector's AI adoption.
item.content:encoded:
A promising AI pilot can look ready for launch and still fail when it meets billing systems, customer authentication rules, or frontline workflows. New research from Adobe and Incisiv suggests that the biggest obstacle for telecommunications companies may not be generating AI ideas—it may be moving them from experimentation into dependable business operations.

Telecommunications respondents said an average of 16 out of every 100 proposed AI initiatives reach production, only slightly above the global average of 15. The largest numerical decline occurs during IT evaluation. Integration has the sharpest proportional drop: 49 proposals enter that stage, but only 31 move forward, representing a 37% reduction.

For small telecom providers and other businesses weighing AI investments, the findings offer a practical warning: Teams should address ownership, integration, measurement, and customer safeguards before a pilot becomes too narrowly defined.

Key takeaways

  • Most AI proposals do not reach production.
  • Only 15% of telecom respondents report having a formal AI owner with a defined role and budget authority.
  • Just 11% measure AI returns comprehensively.
  • Business and IT teams often work in separate or limited ways.
  • Clear success metrics and decision rights can help businesses judge whether a pilot deserves wider investment.

The research does not explain why individual proposals fail or prove that any single management practice causes better AI outcomes. However, it highlights where companies can look for avoidable delays and unresolved questions.

Consider a small internet or telecommunications provider developing an AI assistant for billing inquiries. A demonstration may show that the tool can answer common questions. But deployment requires more than a convincing conversation. The assistant must access accurate billing records, verify a customer’s identity, protect sensitive information, and transfer unresolved issues to a human agent.

If teams postpone those questions until after the pilot, they may discover that the system cannot connect easily to existing software or that customer service staff do not know when to intervene. Bringing IT, customer care, compliance, and operations staff into the project early can expose those requirements while the team can still change the design.

Decision-making also matters. Only 15% of telecommunications respondents in the study report a formal AI owner who has both a defined role and authority over the budget. Other organizations rely on part-time owners, reported by 32% of respondents; committees, reported by 23%; or ad hoc arrangements, reported by 21%. Another 8% say no one has accountability.

For a small business, that gap can create expensive uncertainty. A project may need changes to customer-service software, network systems, data policies, and employee training. If no individual can prioritize those demands or approve additional spending, the initiative can stall even when the technology performs well.

The report also describes a potential “Frozen Middle.” Sixty percent of telecommunications respondents say their organizations are piloting or deploying AI, while 20% are expanding or transforming their use of the technology. Those figures indicate where companies sit in the adoption process, but they do not show whether organizations have stopped progressing or why.

Small business owners can use that distinction when reviewing their own AI programs. A pilot that remains in place for months may provide useful information, but leaders should identify the evidence required to expand it, who can authorize the next stage, and when the company should stop investing.

Measurement presents another challenge. Only 11% of telecommunications respondents say they measure AI returns comprehensively. Many organizations track whether a model ran or whether a customer interaction was completed, but those measures do not necessarily show whether AI improved retention, first-contact resolution, customer experience, network performance, or operating costs.

A small provider should record a baseline before changing its workflow. For a billing assistant, that could include current resolution rates, repeat-contact rates, average handling time, escalation rates, and customer satisfaction. Leaders can then define the improvement the pilot must demonstrate and specify accuracy thresholds and situations that require a handoff to an employee.

Without that baseline, it becomes difficult to separate AI’s impact from changes in pricing, service terms, staffing, or broader operating conditions. A tool may appear successful simply because call volume declined for another reason—or appear ineffective because unrelated service problems increased.

Adobe and Incisiv also compared telecommunications respondents with 342 cross-industry Leaders drawn from a broader survey of 5,633 executives. The Leaders represented about 6% of 5,323 active respondents. They scored 60% higher on organizational structure and 46% higher on workflow transformation, although the report does not establish that these practices caused their greater maturity.

The Leaders were six times more likely to have a formal AI owner with title and budget authority. Nearly half—44%—measured AI returns comprehensively, compared with 11% of telecommunications respondents. Collaborative or integrated business-IT relationships were reported by 80% of Leaders, versus 24% of telecommunications respondents.

The research also points to workplace culture. Destructive patterns involving blame and repeated mistakes affected 37% of telecommunications respondents but fewer than 1% of Leaders. Meanwhile, 42% of Leaders identified finding and empowering internal champions as their most impactful culture move, ahead of executive sponsorship and formal training.

For a small company, an internal champion might be a customer-service supervisor, network engineer, or billing specialist who understands the daily workflow and can identify where AI helps or creates friction. That employee can support adoption, but should not become the sole owner of risk, compliance, or technical integration.

Owners should also avoid treating cross-industry comparisons as a universal blueprint. A small telecom provider may lack the budget, staff, and data infrastructure of a large enterprise. It can still apply the underlying discipline by selecting one priority initiative, assigning a decision-maker, involving affected teams early, and agreeing on evidence before deployment.

For a billing assistant, that could mean limiting the first release to a defined set of questions, documenting identity-verification requirements, setting an escalation rule, and measuring performance against a pre-pilot baseline. Formal reviews should still determine whether the proposal is ready to advance.

Adobe’s original post and the full Adobe and Incisiv report provide additional details on the telecommunications approval funnel, ownership models, measurement practices, and comparisons with cross-industry organizations. For small businesses, the central lesson is straightforward: A successful AI strategy begins before the pilot, when leaders decide who owns the outcome, how the system will fit existing operations, and what results will justify the next dollar of investment.

item.title: What Is the Role of Inventory in Supply Chain Management?
item.dc:creator: John Cook
item.description: Discover the critical role of inventory in supply chain management and how it impacts efficiency, cost control, and customer satisfaction. Learn key strategies for optimizing your inventory to enhance your supply chain performance.
item.content:encoded:
In supply chain management, inventory acts as your safety net, ensuring products are available when customers want them. It prevents stockouts that can lead to lost sales, while also reducing holding costs. To manage inventory effectively, start by tracking real-time data, analyzing demand patterns, and implementing techniques like just-in-time inventory. Each step you take can enhance efficiency and profitability. But what happens when challenges arise, and how can you tackle them?

Key Takeaways

  • Inventory ensures products are available to meet customer demand, preventing stockouts and enhancing satisfaction.
  • Effective inventory management minimizes holding costs, reducing waste and increasing profitability.
  • Real-time visibility into inventory levels enables informed decision-making and quick adaptation to market changes.
  • Accurate inventory levels enhance resource allocation, improving overall supply chain efficiency.
  • Implementing advanced techniques helps align inventory with actual demand, balancing ordering and holding costs.

Why Inventory Matters in Supply Chain Management

Inventory matters in supply chain management because it directly impacts your ability to meet customer demand and maintain profitability. Understanding the importance of inventory helps you prevent stockouts, which can lead to lost sales and unhappy customers.

Effective inventory management can also minimize holding costs and reduce waste, potentially boosting your profits by up to 10%.

To enhance your supply chain operations, keep accurate inventory levels. Discrepancies can result in inefficient resource allocation and increased carrying costs.

Real-time visibility into your inventory allows you to make informed decisions and quickly adapt to market changes.

Consider implementing advanced techniques like Just-in-Time (JIT) or Economic Order Quantity (EOQ). These methods can help you balance ordering and holding costs, ensuring your inventory aligns closely with actual demand.

Key Inventory Management Techniques for Greater Efficiency

Consider Just-In-Time (JIT) inventory management to reduce excess stock, aligning inventory arrivals with production schedules. This requires accurate demand forecasting and reliable suppliers.

Use Safety Stock Management as a buffer against unexpected demand changes, ensuring product availability.

Finally, adopt Multi-Echelon Inventory Management to optimize stock levels across various locations, enhancing responsiveness to demand fluctuations.

Inventory Management Challenges and Their Solutions

When managing inventory, it’s crucial to recognize the challenges that can disrupt your supply chain. Demand variability and inaccurate forecasting can lead to stockouts or excess inventory, impacting cash flow and customer satisfaction.

To tackle this, consider adopting inventory management models that enhance your demand forecasting accuracy.

Supply chain disruptions, like natural disasters or geopolitical events, require you to develop robust strategies for inventory flow. Implementing advanced technologies, such as AI and data analytics, can help optimize your inventory levels and reduce waste.

Moreover, maintaining real-time visibility and collaborating with suppliers guarantees timely replenishment.

Regular inventory audits and the Plan–Do–Check–Act (PDCA) framework facilitate continuous improvement, helping you adapt to ongoing challenges.

How to Overcome Inventory Challenges and Balance Supply and Demand?

To effectively overcome inventory challenges and balance supply and demand, you need to focus on accurate demand forecasting. Start by utilizing advanced analytics and AI-driven models to predict consumer behavior, ensuring you adjust stock levels dynamically.

Remember, the importance of inventory management in supply chain can’t be overstated. Implement Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) to minimize costs by balancing ordering and holding expenses, especially for products with stable demand.

Regular inventory audits and real-time monitoring systems should be part of your strategy to enhance visibility and accuracy. This helps address demand variability and reduces waste.

Collaborate closely with your suppliers to align lead times and order sizes, making your inventory flow more responsive to market changes. By taking these steps, you can effectively manage your inventory, prevent stockouts or excess, and maintain a smoother supply chain operation.

Emerging Trends Shaping the Future of Inventory Management

As technology evolves, you’re likely to see several emerging trends that will shape the future of inventory management. These trends can enhance the role of inventory in supply chain management, making it more efficient and responsive.

Here are four key developments to watch:

  • Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) will help you predict demand and optimize stock levels in real-time.
  • Just-in-Time (JIT) practices can reduce waste, requiring strong supplier collaboration and precise forecasting.
  • Internet of Things (IoT) technology allows you to monitor inventory continuously, enhancing visibility and enabling proactive management.
  • A focus on sustainability encourages eco-friendly practices, leading to Closed-loop Supply Chain (CLSC) strategies.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Are the 4 Types of Inventory?

The four types of inventory are raw materials, work-in-progress (WIP), finished goods, and maintenance, repair, and operations (MRO) supplies.

Raw materials are the basic components. WIP includes partially completed products. Finished goods are ready for sale, and MRO supplies keep your machinery running.

To manage these effectively, regularly assess your stock levels, track turnover rates, and streamline ordering processes.

This way, you’ll maintain efficiency and avoid production delays.

What Is the Golden Rule for Inventory?

The golden rule for inventory is to balance supply and demand effectively. You need to maintain stock levels that meet customer needs without creating excess or shortages.

To do this, regularly assess your inventory, use techniques like Economic Order Quantity to determine ideal order sizes, and implement real-time monitoring for better visibility.

What Are the 7 Pillars of Logistics?

The seven pillars of logistics are Planning, Transportation, Inventory Management, Warehousing, Order Fulfillment, Information Management, and Customer Service.

Start by planning your logistics strategies to optimize resources. Next, manage transportation efficiently to move goods effectively.

Balance your inventory levels to meet demand without excess. Guarantee proper warehousing for storage and distribution.

Focus on timely order fulfillment, leverage data for information management, and prioritize customer service to maintain satisfaction.

What Is the Main Purpose of Inventory Management in a Supply Chain?

The main purpose of inventory management in a supply chain is to balance supply and demand effectively.

To achieve this, you should regularly assess inventory levels, anticipate demand fluctuations, and adjust stock accordingly.

Aim to minimize costs by avoiding overstocking and stockouts, which can hurt customer satisfaction.

Use technology for real-time visibility, and integrate decisions across the supply chain to enhance operational efficiency and reduce waste, ensuring you meet customer needs promptly.

Conclusion

To conclude, effective inventory management is essential for your supply chain’s success. To enhance efficiency, implement techniques like just-in-time and ABC analysis. Tackle common challenges by adopting inventory tracking software and regularly reviewing stock levels. Always stay adaptable to market changes by forecasting demand accurately. As trends evolve, keep learning and adjusting your strategies. By focusing on these steps, you’ll not only meet customer needs but also boost your bottom line. Start optimizing your inventory today.
